title: Jaw or mandibular breathing in the last day or hours

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: Public sources describe recognized patterns but do not supply firsthand room texture.
The record must not be used to diagnose, time, or manage a particular death.
Treatment, legal, ritual, and emergency decisions remain local and must be handled by qualified teams or relevant authorities.

moment.plain_scene: A dying person’s mouth may open and the jaw may move with breaths, producing a pattern that looks different from ordinary breathing and can alarm people at the bedside.
ordinary_language_queries: jaw moving when breathing near death

content_layers.observation_text: Public and professional sources describe mouth opening and jaw movement with breathing near the end of life; professional sources treat respiration with mandibular movement as a specific late sign but also warn against using signs in isolation.
content_layers.source_synthesis: NCI, Marie Curie, PCNOW, and Hospice UK support the record while preserving a strong prediction boundary.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: The vocabulary matters here because families search visually: “jaw moving,” “fish mouth,” “mouth open.” The glossary term should meet those phrases without making the witness become a diagnostician.

what_this_is_not: not proof that death will occur at a precise time
not a diagnosis by family observation
not interchangeable with every gasping or mouth movement
not an instruction to reposition or medicate
uncertainties: Different sources use different naming and timing language.
A lay witness may not distinguish mandibular breathing from other irregular patterns.
The record needs clinician review to prevent overconfident timing claims.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should describe jaw breathing as one possible late breathing change and tell worried readers to contact the care team.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should capture explanation language for a pattern that can look frightening even when expected.
language_notes: Include “jaw breathing” as search language and “respiration with mandibular movement” as professional crosswalk.
Do not lead with “fish mouth” except as a query alias because it can sound dehumanizing.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the v2 witnessed-moment schema. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, legal, cultural, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical safety review and ensure any lay surface directs urgent or worried readers to qualified local support.
